title: Delegates, Func, and Action (typed method references and multicast)
hook: A delegate is a type that holds a reference to a method with a matching signature. When a message queue handler needs to ack, log metrics, and route poison messages, you bind those methods to delegates instead of calling them by name everywhere.

blocks.text: A **delegate** is a Common Language Runtime (CLR) type that represents a reference to a method with a particular parameter list and return type. You declare the shape once, then create instances that point at static or instance methods. Unlike JavaScript, where every function is already a value, a C# method becomes a value only when you assign it to a delegate. **Func** and **Action** are built-in generic delegate types for the most common shapes: Func returns a value; Action returns void.

entries.plainDefinition: A sealed type that stores a method reference plus an optional target object for instance methods.
A generic delegate whose last type parameter is the return type. Func<int, bool> takes an int and returns bool.
A generic delegate that returns void (no return value). Action<string> takes one string argument.
A delegate whose invocation list contains more than one method. Combining with + or += calls each handler in order.

blocks.text: Delegates are how C# expresses callbacks, event handlers, and middleware pipelines. A RabbitMQ consumer that runs ack, metrics, and poison routing as separate methods stays testable because each step is a typed delegate, not a string you eval. The signature includes the **return type** — a common interview trap is assuming overload rules apply; they do not. Two methods that differ only by return type cannot share one delegate type.

blocks.title: When to use a custom delegate type
blocks.body: Prefer Func and Action for generic plumbing. Use a named delegate when the type name is part of your public contract — especially for domain events like MessageHandler or TryParseId with ref/out parameters.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Declare or choose a delegate type
items.body: Use Func/Action for common shapes, or declare a custom delegate that names the contract.

items.title: Bind a method group
items.body: Assign a compatible static or instance method. The compiler stores the target object for instance methods.

items.title: Combine for multicast
items.body: Use += or + to append handlers. Each combination allocates a new invocation list.

items.title: Invoke safely
items.body: Copy the delegate field to a local variable before Invoke to avoid a race with unsubscription. Use GetInvocationList to isolate handler failures.

blocks.title: Delegates in C# vs JS/TS functions
rows: Methods become values only when bound to a delegate
Every function is already an object you can pass around
CLR validates signature at compile time and runtime
JS has no compile-time checks; TS checks are erased at runtime
Built into delegate types with + and +=
You build your own array of listeners
Not part of JS function identity; TS includes it in types

blocks.title: Public delegate field instead of event
blocks.body: A public delegate property lets any caller assign null and wipe every handler. Use the event keyword when outsiders should only += and -=.

blocks.title: Assuming -= removes all matching handlers
blocks.body: -= removes one matching entry from the end of the invocation list, not every equal handler. Loop carefully when cleaning up.

interviewTakeaways: Delegate signature includes return type; overload resolution does not apply.
Func/Action are the default; custom delegates name a contract.
Multicast is synchronous; one throw stops the rest unless you walk GetInvocationList.
Snapshot the delegate field to a local before invoke to avoid a race with unsubscription.
commonPitfalls: Declaring a public delegate field so callers can assign null and wipe every handler.
Assuming -= removes every equal handler; it removes one matching entry from the end.
Capturing loop variables in handlers subscribed inside a foreach over deliveries.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript functions are values you pass freely. C# methods become values only when bound to a delegate. JavaScript has no built-in multicast type — you compose arrays of functions yourself.
type Handler = (id: string) => void is erased at runtime. A C# delegate remains metadata the CLR checks when you invoke it.
